issues.failure_explanation: Scalable exactness only constrains q near diagonal values of the form λf*(a), with λ in the specified interval; it imposes no condition at an arbitrary value f(a). Likewise, affine exactness constrains diagonal values only in the range of f*. A smooth q can agree with the required exact rule on those constrained values and be altered elsewhere, so the claimed error estimate for every C^2 function does not follow. The same overreach makes the expansion in cor:added-1 invalid when f(a) is not the target diagonal value.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restrict the conclusions to functions whose value f(a) lies in the diagonal-value region actually controlled by the relevant exactness hypothesis, or strengthen the hypotheses so that q and its needed derivatives are controlled at every possible diagonal value.
issues.overall_effect: The paper has not shown that scalable or affine exactness makes a two-point nonlinear rule no worse than the trapezoidal rule on completely arbitrary functions; the corresponding unrestricted local expansion is also unsupported.
issues.title: Exactness on a restricted family does not control arbitrary diagonal values
issues.why_classification: The repair is conceptually contained but requires a genuine restriction or strengthening of the hypotheses and withdraws the stated guarantee for all C^2 functions.

diagnostic_evidence.quote:
Let $f^*:\Rset\to R\subseteq\Rset$ be bijective with inverse function
$f^*{}^{-1}$

is symmetric and affinely exact on $f^*$ and
has $o(h^4)$ errors for $f\in C^4(\Rset)$.

issues.failure_explanation: The inverse f*^{-1} is defined only on R, so q1 is undefined when either sampled value lies outside R, although the theorem claims an error result for every real-valued C^4 function. It is also a 0/0 expression when f0=f1, including the constant affine transform α=0 required by affine exactness. The exponential specialization has the same missing-domain and equal-value problems and therefore is not a map R^2→R as stipulated earlier; in particular, its asserted quasilinearity for all real scalars is not meaningful at zero or on arbitrary sign patterns.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Specify continuous diagonal values, restrict admissible integrands so all samples lie in R, and state an appropriate domain for q; alternatively, provide a globally defined sufficiently smooth extension and verify that it retains the claimed accuracy.
issues.overall_effect: The construction does not, as written, define the claimed quadrature on all admissible inputs, and neither its full affine-exactness assertion nor its unrestricted C^4 error guarantee is well posed.
issues.title: The construction is not defined on its stated input domain
issues.why_classification: Diagonal values are locally repairable, but resolving the range problem requires either a substantive restriction of the advertised C^4 scope or a new extension construction.

Since $q_1$ is a symmetric affinely exact non-linear quadrature formula, its
partial derivatives at each order are given by Corollary \ref{cor:pders}.

issues.failure_explanation: The proof differentiates q1 through third order, but the hypotheses do not ensure that f*^{-1}, and hence q1, has those derivatives at diagonal values. For the allowed target f*(x)=x^3, with F*(x)=x^4/4, the inverse is a cube root and q1 is not smoothly differentiable at sample value zero. Taking a=0 and f(x)=x, direct substitution into q2 gives an error proportional to h^2 with nonzero coefficient, rather than o(h^4). Thus the stated fourth-order conclusion is false under the theorem's hypotheses.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add nondegeneracy and regularity hypotheses sufficient to make the inverse and q1 smoothly differentiable to the required order on all relevant diagonal values, and then redo the Taylor justification under those hypotheses.
issues.overall_effect: The central higher-order construction does not attain its claimed Newton–Cotes-level accuracy for all bijective target functions covered by the theorem.
issues.title: Bijectivity alone does not provide the smoothness needed for fourth-order accuracy
issues.why_classification: A comparable theorem may survive after a meaningful but contained restriction such as excluding critical points of f*, but the present advertised class of bijections must be narrowed.

issues.failure_explanation: Polynomials having different degrees does not generally imply that their vectors of values at a finite set of nodes are linearly independent. Consequently, the stated reason for existence and uniqueness of the coefficient solution is invalid, leaving the identification with the Newton–Cotes rule unproved at that step.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Supply the short node-specific nonsingularity argument: a linear combination vanishing at the listed nodes has zero constant and linear coefficients, hence a double root at zero; its remaining listed roots and the induced condition at one force the polynomial, and therefore all coefficients, to vanish.
